notes.title: Why networks exist: origins and business need
notes.caption: Networks did not start with computers. A deal is only as fast as the information behind it.
keys: Networks did not start with computers — they started with people signalling, long before any device.
Human, mechanical, then electronic signalling were used by people, communities, and companies to send a message farther and faster.
Business = exchange of information: a deal is only as fast as the information behind it.

notes.title: Naming, addressing and regulation: directory to DNS
notes.caption: Before DNS, the directory was a telephone book run by government. Names are delegated, addresses allocated by region.
keys: Before DNS, the directory was a telephone book run by government, used by telecom companies, businesses, and people.
ICANN, RIRs, and IP blocks: names are delegated hierarchically and addresses allocated by region, so networks can find each other.
FCC, TRAI, IETF, IEEE, and 3GPP regulate telecom companies, spectrum, and standards.

notes.title: Hardware supply and the NIC endpoint
notes.caption: Silicon becomes a chip, a chip becomes a vendor's device, and that device reaches a customer through the NIC.
keys: Silicon becomes a chip, and a chip becomes a vendor's device that a telecom company or business can buy and use.
Intel, Broadcom, and Nvidia supply hardware controlled by software, for cloud, OEMs, telcos, and government labs.
That device only reaches a customer through the NIC endpoint, on PCI, with a driver and operating system.

notes.title: The NIC and kernel stack, plus out-of-band management
notes.caption: Two lanes that must not be confused: the data lane and the management lane.
keys: A customer's traffic goes through the NIC interface, driver, kernel stack, net device, and TCP/IP.
Two lanes must not be confused: the data lane carries traffic, the management lane manages the device, even when it is down.
Out-of-band to BMC, then CLI, web, or API, lets a company manage a device while its data lane is down, so trading can resume faster and market trust is kept.

notes.title: Building, operating and approving a product
notes.caption: A product closes the loop: built, tested, sold, bought from vendors, gated by approval.
keys: A product is built by engineering and operations, tested, sold to customers, and bought through vendors who buy silicon.
FCC approval is the gate: equipment certification for routers and phones, and a broadband speed report, before market entry.
That gate depends on every card before it — origins, naming, hardware, and the NIC stack.

notes.title: Univescal product / Business (network / Standards
notes.subject: Systems evolution
keys: A universal product is a spectrum: tech, manufacturing, software, and business together, carrying four things in parallel.
Four parallel flows (communication): communication → trade → speed → Tech, and that speed is itself a technology advantage.
Cross Flow (physical, informational, financial, rules) plus Tech Integration across the flow turns a good into a full value chain, connected.

notes.title: Govt Layer (TO controll public
notes.subject: Systems evolution
keys: Government is added as a unifying layer across all flows, from source to consumer, to control the public.

Global Oversight → International standard bodies → Regional Regulation → National Enforcement → Industry Standards → market flow, with bodies that have different legal powers, not one hierarchy (R14).
Government networks are built like the market in reverse: series, manufacturers, vendors, implementers, buyers, public, with government controllers closing the loop.

notes.title: UI frameworks Evolution
notes.subject: Systems evolution
keys: The interface is the same question in every era: medium, public vs private frameworks, architecture, and what it feels like to use.
From hardware only, to punch cards and CLI, to GUI desktops, to browsers, to mobile apps and cloud backends, to real-time XR and AI interfaces.
Frameworks belong to different categories — Bootstrap is CSS, React/AngularJS are UI frameworks, X11/Motif are windowing systems — and REST/GraphQL/gRPC are API styles, not UI frameworks.

notes.title: Tech leadership Era
notes.caption: Who leads each era: org structure, tech strategy, and leadership mindset — telegraph to 5G & AI, with the post-2000 completion labelled [Added].
keys: Leadership is three questions in each era: org structure, tech strategy, and leadership mindset.
Telegraph: centralised, protocols, link state. Distribution: a centralised team managing decentralisation, interoperability protocols.
The original page stops at 2000, at hypergrowth — Eras 3–5 on this card are labelled [Added] completion, proposed where interpretation.

notes.title: Eras UI Frameworks + Hardware controlled / SW
notes.caption: The same six eras, three lenses: interface, control, and how it is paid for — from PTT duration to API Token.
keys: The same six eras read three ways: interface/hardware control, private business controller, and payment model.
Payment moves from duration, to chargeback, to licence, to advertising/subscription, to SaaS + usage, to API Token.
ICANN, IETF and W3C are distinguished: allocation, Internet standards, and web standards — not one body.

notes.title: Project scheduler
notes.caption: One scheduler model: tasks, resources, and who allocates them fairly — electricity, networking, and business projects.
keys: A scheduler allocates resources fairly and efficiently — it is not just a timetable.
The same model holds for electricity (ISO), networking (ISP), and business projects (agency, company, banks, consortia).
Schedulers are distinguished by function: ISO/RTO, ICANN, ISP, and VISA/SWIFT do different allocation work.
